name: Núi Bà Đen (Black Virgin Mountain)
alternateNames: "Sun Mountain" (as Larry may have called it)
summary: An isolated mountain rising from the plain near Tây Ninh in southern Vietnam, site of significant U.S. military activity including a signal and relay presence on its summit. Larry's association became much more specific in his 2026-08-13 comments: he stood search-and-rescue duty at the Special Forces camp there — call sign Body Jab 42 — near the old French fort, photographed a rocket launcher being mounted on the summit (VN-0006), remembers Sgt. Lowry stationed on top, and places the "450 civilians" accusation here at the very end of his tour.
larrysRecollection: Larry remembers being on or associated with the mountain — he may have referred to it as something sounding like "Sun Mountain." In his 2026-08-13 comments he described standing search-and-rescue duty at the Special Forces camp (call sign Body Jab 42; his own search-and-rescue call sign was Tay Ninh), running around the French fort to relay a helicopter's warning, and being extracted by Rosethorn 007 on the day of the accusation. He writes the name as "Nui Ba Din."
researchNotes: The mountain's location is settled geography; what remains unverified is the nature and dates of Larry's association with it. His 2026-08-13 testimony adds corroborating texture — the French fort matches the mountain's documented colonial ruins, and the two green berets visible in VN-0006 match the Special Forces presence he describes — but the photo's location is itself his identification, so the classification stays as recollection pending documentary support. The "Sun Mountain" name should be checked against period American nicknames. Special Forces and signal activity on the summit during 1964-1965 should be researched, including any Sergeant Lowry/Lowery and the camp call sign Body Jab 42 (see research/events/450-civilians-nui-ba-den.md). Research sweep 2026-08-13: the official Army history (Kelly, U.S. Army Special Forces 1961–1971) documents a CIDG camp at Núi Bà Đen itself in October 1964 manned by a half-size SF element — 1 officer, 5 enlisted, ~175 CIDG strikers — matching Larry's memory of a skeleton crew; the summit was taken by SF helicopter assault in May 1964, Detachment B-32 ran Tây Ninh province from January 1965, and the well-known 121st Signal Battalion relay ('Granite Romeo Tango') only arrived February 1966, so Larry's radio-relay window falls in the sparsely documented SF-relay period. 'French Fort on the back side of Nui Ba Den' is attested verbatim as an American place name. On this documentary fit the association is upgraded to plausible; direct confirmation of Larry's presence awaits his NPRC records.
